title: Inclusive Design & User Research 🧪
description: Go beyond compliance: involve people with disabilities in design, usability testing, and co‑creation.

slides.title: From Compliance to Delight ✨
slides.content:
WCAG sets the minimum bar. To create truly inclusive products, you must go beyond the checklist.

- Involve people with disabilities throughout the design process.
- Understand their goals, frustrations, and workarounds.
- Co‑design solutions with them, not just for them.

Accessibility is not about ticking boxes – it's about enabling equal experiences.

quizData.question: What is the primary advantage of involving users with disabilities in usability testing?

options.text: You discover real‑world barriers that compliance checklists miss

quizData.explanation: Real users reveal pain points and context that automated tools and guidelines can't capture.

slides.title: Recruiting Participants with Disabilities 👥
slides.content:
Many organizations struggle to find testers. Solutions:

- Partner with disability organizations (local or national).
- Use specialized recruitment agencies (e.g., Fable, Knowbility).
- Build a panel of users from your customer base (ask for accessibility interest in surveys).
- Offer fair compensation – respect their time and expertise.

Aim for diversity: different disabilities, assistive tech, and experience levels.

quizData.question: Why should you recruit participants with a variety of disabilities?

options.text: Different disabilities encounter different barriers; one size does not fit all

quizData.explanation: A screen reader user, a low‑vision user, and a switch user will each reveal unique issues.

slides.title: Conducting Accessible Usability Tests 🧪
slides.content:
Your testing environment and script must be accessible:

- Use accessible remote testing tools (ensure they work with screen readers).
- Allow participants to use their own assistive technology (don't force a specific tool).
- Ask open‑ended tasks, not step‑by‑step instructions.
- Record consent, observe silently, and take notes on barriers.
- Debrief and ask about their experience.

Test early – paper prototypes and wireframes can be tested with screen readers.

slides.title: Co‑design & Participatory Design 🎨
slides.content:
Take inclusion further:

- Invite people with disabilities to design workshops.
- Use inclusive brainstorming techniques (verbal, tactile).
- Prototype together, get immediate feedback.
- Empower them as designers, not just test subjects.

This approach leads to innovations that delight everyone.

quizData.question: What is the benefit of co‑designing with users with disabilities?

options.text: It brings lived experience into the solution, leading to more innovative and inclusive outcomes

quizData.explanation: Co‑design leverages the expertise of users who navigate barriers daily.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Start small – one test per sprint
Even one usability session with a screen reader user per month can revolutionize your team's empathy and output.
